newsitem.title: SPAIN: New Iberia boss pledges culture change.
newsitem.headline: New Iberia boss pledges culture change.

text.p: Spain's state-owned airline Iberia, which expects to return to profit this year after eight years in the red, is preparing to be a more aggressive competitor in both the domestic and international markets, chairman Xabier de Irala said.
"We will establish a new, aggressive commercial policy," he told journalists late on Thursday.
"The company was culturally not prepared to cut prices and compete...A lot of things are going to change at Iberia," he said in his first meeting with foreign journalists since taking office in July.

Iberia has already fired the first shots in a domestic fare war by cutting prices by up to 25 percent on a number of key trunk routes earlier this month, a move which raised howls of protest from its privately-owned competitors.
"Iberia is going to join the competition game at full throttle. We will defend our leadership with all the weapons available," he said.
The flag carrier was caught out when competitors were allowed into its domestic market in 1994 but now that it had returned to profit it could react, he said.
"We will continue to reduce costs and improve our competitiveness," he added. "Iberia is now in a situation of unstable equilibrium and our first task has to be to consolidate our profitability."
The second task was to tie up with ideally a European and a U.S. partner to form part of a global alliance.
Iberia has been talking to potential partners for some time and Irala mentioned no new names.

"A strategic alliance is absolutely necessary...an alliance that can consolidate the company's position in Europe and, as we have a strategic gap in North America, therefore we need a U.S. alliance too."
Joining the British Airways and American Airlines partnership would be an attractive option, he said.
"If it works it's a winner, but it is an alternative and not the only one. There are well advanced talks and the options are open."

Iberia will eventually be privatised and ideally partnerships should be made with a view to the other sides buying a stake in the company, even if the deal was initially a code-sharing agreement with cost savings and synergies all round.

Iberia made a 10.9 billion peseta ($84 million) pre-tax profit in the first eight months of the year and, although it is now revising its end year forecast, is confident the net final figure will not be far short of this amount. ($1=129.6 Peseta)
